stories.h: Gemini API managed agents default to 3.6 Flash with environment hooks
stories.s: This update formalizes safer, cost-aware autonomous workflows and widens access for experimentation by enabling new safety and governance features in managed agents.
b: Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default for Gemini API Managed Agents.
Environment hooks let you block, lint, or audit tool calls inside the sandbox via a configurable setup (e.g., .agents/hooks.json).
Budget controls, scheduled triggers, and free tier access are now available for managed agents.
To cap resource use, max_total_tokens can be set in agent_config; when reached, execution pauses with status “incomplete” and the state can be resumed later.
body: Google’s blog post on Gemini API Managed Agents announces that Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default for managed agents, building on prior updates that introduced background tasks and remote server integrations.

A key upgrade is the introduction of environment hooks, which allow developers to run pre-tool and post-tool execution scripts inside the agent’s sandbox. The documentation notes that you can define hooks in a file like .agents/hooks.json and tailor actions for specific tools or events.

The post also highlights new governance features such as budget controls and scheduled triggers, along with free tier access for projects without active billing, making it easier to experiment with agentic workflows.

Crucially, the system supports token budgeting via max_total_tokens in agent_config. If the limit is hit, execution pauses and returns an incomplete status, preserving the environment so you can resume with a new budget and a previous_interaction_id. The update also reinforces the ability to explicitly select models through agent_config.model, including options like gemini-3.5-flash-lite.
srcTitles: Gemini API Managed Agents: 3.6 Flash, hooks, and more
The Weirdness of Agents
FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills

stories.h: Samsung chip workers jump ship to SK Hynix after bigger bonuses
stories.s: The exodus signals a high-stakes talent war that could determine who leads AI memory chips and how quickly supply and pricing shift for AI accelerators.
b: SK Hynix is paying about $476,000 per employee this year, mostly in cash, to lure talent from Samsung
Samsung’s bonuses by division vary: memory division about $400,000 per employee vs. foundry division about $135,000
81.5% of employees in Samsung’s foundry division reportedly want to move to another company within two years, and more than 200 union members left for SK Hynix over the past four months

In H1 2026 SK Hynix added 2,152 employees to staff the expansion, and both firms topped $1 trillion in market value in May, with SK Hynix briefly dethroning Samsung as Korea’s most valuable company in June
body: MIT Technology Review reports that Samsung’s chip workers are jumping ship to SK Hynix as the AI hardware boom fuels a fierce talent war. Lee, an engineer in Samsung’s semiconductor division, describes coworkers applying to SK Hynix and says his team lead tells them to jump ship to SK Hynix, a message that has spread through the office as workers seek better pay and prospects.

The report notes that Samsung struck a deal in May to pay out 10.5% of the semiconductor division’s operating profits to employees as bonuses for 10 years, mostly in stock that vests over three years. In contrast, SK Hynix is paying a much larger upfront package: roughly $476,000 per employee this year, mostly in cash, a figure that dwarfs Samsung’s payouts. Within Samsung, bonuses vary by division: the memory division pays about $400,000 per employee this year, while the foundry division pays roughly $135,000.

Labor dynamics are central to the tale. Samsung’s labor union talks have yielded gains in other areas, but workers say the discrepancy in bonuses helps explain the defections. The Samsung labor union chief, Choi Seung-ho, has said that more than 200 members have left for SK Hynix in the past four months, and a June survey reported that 81.5% of foundry division employees want to move to another company within two years. Some employees also discuss their plans on Blind, an anonymous workplace forum, underscoring a broad morale challenge at Samsung’s chip plants.

The broader market context adds pressure to this talent war. MIT Technology Review notes that SK Hynix now leads the global market for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, a technology central to AI accelerators, while Samsung has been scrambling to catch up. Both companies topped $1 trillion in market value in May, and SK Hynix briefly dethroned Samsung as Korea’s most valuable company in June. To staff expansion tied to this growth, SK Hynix reported adding 2,152 employees in the first half of 2026. In parallel, the AI spending boom and China’s progress in advanced chipmaking have fed a stock-market reaction: Bloomberg, via Techmeme, reported that South Korea’s KOSPI fell more than 11%, with Samsung down around 11% and SK Hynix down about 12%.

What happens next could reshape the AI hardware supply chain. MIT Technology Review frames the outcome as a race to dominate the next generation of HBMs, with the winner potentially locking in talent, boosting production capacity, and influencing pricing as demand for AI chips remains volatile.
srcTitles: Samsung’s chip workers are jumping ship to rival SK Hynix

stories.h: Runlayer sues Rippling over alleged IP theft in MCP gateway dispute
stories.s: The case shows how long enterprise AI trials can reveal confidential IP and fuel copycat competition in the growing MCP gateway market.
b: Runlayer alleges Rippling copied its MCP gateway IP after a nearly year-long product trial that included access to Runlayer's roadmap and source code.
Both sides signed a mutual NDA and a product trial agreement barring IP copying; Runlayer says price negotiations ended the trial.
Rippling confirmed it is launching its own MCP gateway and denied Runlayer's misappropriation claims.
Runlayer has engaged Sullivan Cromwell; Runlayer previously raised about $42 million from investors including Khosla Ventures and Felicis.
body: Runlayer, a startup that offers a secure Model Context Protocol gateway for AI models and agents, has filed a lawsuit against HR software company Rippling, the complaint seen by TechCrunch shows. The suit paints a cautionary tale for enterprises buying AI infrastructure, noting how extensive trials can expose intellectual property.

The complaint describes nearly a year of engineering collaboration during a product trial, conducted under a mutual non-disclosure agreement and a trial agreement that included a clause forbidding copying Runlayer’s IP. The two parties could not agree on a price, which contributed to ending the trial on terms unfavorable to Runlayer.

Runlayer alleges that an internal Rippling message indicated a project to build essentially a clone of Runlayer, describing it as “almost a 1 to 1 copy of Runlayer.” The claim is that Rippling’s evaluation involved confidential information that should have remained protected by the NDA and trial agreement.

Rippling confirmed it is launching its own MCP gateway and told TechCrunch that it denies Runlayer’s misappropriation claims. A Rippling spokesperson said the company is building a gateway “for connecting AI tools to business data using only our proprietary information – we have every reason to win in this market.” The company also said it takes IP protection seriously.

Runlayer has retained the white-shoe law firm Sullivan Cromwell, adding to the visibility of the case. The broader enterprise AI market for MCP gateways has been crowded since Anthropic opened MCP as an open-source protocol in 2024, and Runlayer had raised a total of about $42 million from investors including Khosla Ventures and Felicis prior to the dispute.

The suit is described as shedding light on the challenges of selling complex AI infrastructure into the enterprise, where long, hands-on trials often determine whether a product wins or loses in a competitive market.
srcTitles: MCP startup Runlayer accuses Rippling of stealing its product idea

There is no investment component to AWS’s involvement in the deal, but AWS is expected to commit significant resources to RSI’s needs and co‑develop infrastructure tailored for these types of companies, according to Jason Bennett, AWS VP for startups and venture capital.

RSI’s leadership positions self‑improvement as a potential inflection point for AI progress, though coverage notes that the exact requirements and timelines remain ambiguous as more labs pursue the idea. Socher emphasized tangible progress, telling TechCrunch that users could see “the earliest examples before the end of the year,” with a concrete reveal around October.

Five models launched in the past year (four speech generation, one speech‑to‑text); three generation models open‑sourced, latest S2.1 Pro is API‑based and paid
The company automated its voice‑ownership DMCA takedown flow to under 3 minutes for consented voice removals; creators can submit proof of ownership for fast removal
body: Fish Audio, a Palo Alto startup, announced a $50 million seed round led by Coreline Ventures and Capital Today to expand its library of AI voice models for creators and enterprises. The company aims to support a broad range of use cases from expressive character voices to automated customer interactions, with a library that currently features more than 15,000 natural language controls.

Since its public launch last year, Fish Audio has grown to over 8 million users across its open‑source and hosted offerings and reports annual recurring revenue of about $21 million. The startup has rolled out five models over the past year—four speech generation models and one speech‑to‑text model—and has open‑sourced three generation models, while the latest S2.1 Pro model is available only through its paid API.

Fish Audio’s CEO and co‑founder Rissa Cao indicated a broad portfolio of voice applications, with customers including companies like HeyGen, Sanas and Plaud that use its voices for different needs—realism for avatars, expressiveness for games, or natural voices for voice agents.

The company has faced earlier concerns when creators claimed their voices were uploaded without consent; Fish Audio has since automated its DMCA removal flow, allowing creators to submit a sample or contract to prove ownership and have their voice taken down within minutes. Investors stressed that consent, transparency, and clear licensing are essential to building trust in community‑driven voice ecosystems.

Looking ahead, Fish Audio plans to release an audio understanding model this year and is also working on a speech‑to‑speech model, as it competes in a crowded market with players like ElevenLabs and Krisp.
srcTitles: Fish Audio raises $52M seed to build AI voice models for creators and enterprises

body: Marco Tedesco’s piece on State of the Planet explores what responsible AI should look like, contributing to a broader discussion about governance and ethics in AI deployment.

Separately, The Harvard Crimson article argues that Cambridge schools need a new AI policy and suggests what that policy should look like, illustrating a school‑level demand for governance around AI use.

Together, the two pieces reflect a growing push for governance frameworks around AI in educational settings, indicating that schools and universities are becoming a focal point for policy development in this area.

Editorial coverage indicates that policy discussions in education are intensifying and that clearer guidelines for AI use in classrooms are likely to follow as institutions grapple with how to integrate AI responsibly.

stories.s: It signals tighter corporate AI budgets, potentially slowing enterprise adoption and affecting vendors that rely on business contracts.
b: Outlets reporting the story: WRAL.com and ABC News.
Headline centers on AI tokenmaxxing fading as workplaces look to cut tech spending.
The framing presents a broader trend in enterprise tech budgets rather than actions by a single company.
body: WRAL reports a trend described in the headline that AI tokenmaxxing is fading as workplaces cut tech spending.
ABC News published a similar report, framing the shift as part of broader corporate budget tightening on technology.
Both outlets use the term tokenmaxxing to describe changes in enterprise AI spending patterns, and focus on budget cuts rather than specific deployments.
No numbers, dates, or company names are provided in the materials available in this coverage, and the stories treat the trend as a general industry move rather than a single incident.
